title: Tian Ji Wins the Horse Race
text:
In the state of Qi in the 4th century BC, the general Tian Ji often raced horses against King Wei and the princes for large wagers. Each side entered three horses, one from each of three grades: top, middle and lowest. The king's horses in each grade were a little better than Tian Ji's, so Tian Ji kept losing.

Sima Qian tells that Tian Ji had recently taken in Sun Bin, a strategist who had been crippled and branded by a jealous rival in the state of Wei and smuggled out to Qi. Sun Bin watched the races and noticed that the horses of each grade were not very far apart. He told Tian Ji to bet heavily, promising him victory.

His plan changed only the order. Tian Ji would run his lowest horse against the king's best, his best against the king's middle horse, and his middle horse against the king's lowest. Tian Ji followed the advice. He lost the first race badly but won the other two, and with them a thousand pieces of gold.

Impressed, Tian Ji introduced Sun Bin to King Wei. The king questioned him on the art of war and made him his military adviser.
lesson: You do not have to be stronger everywhere to win. Decide where to concede and where to concentrate, and match your strengths against the other side's weaker points.
people: Tian Ji, Sun Bin, King Wei of Qi
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 65
